Mar–Jul 2026 ·one desktop, no cloud services

A research paper,
read to you by two people.

Drop a PDF in. Get back a thirty-six minute conversation between two voices who have actually read it — one asking, one explaining, and then the other way round.

I am dyslexic. Reading a dense twenty-page paper and listening to two people discuss it are very different amounts of work, and only one of them is available on a walk. The PDF handling, the speech synthesis and every artifact stay on my own machine. The two drafting stages call a hosted model, which is the one place that is not true.

How it works

Four stages, each leaving something the next one can check

I drive it from a chat window. Each stage writes files to disk that I can read before the next stage runs, so nothing happens in one opaque jump from PDF to audio.

STAGE 1

Read the PDF

A small Python service pulls text out of the PDF and tags every paragraph with an invisible marker. A tagged paragraph is what the rest of this page calls anchored: it has a stable name later stages can point at.

→ paper.md + paper.spans.json
STAGE 2

Find the sections

The paper's real structure gets annotated onto the paragraphs from stage 1. Abstract, method, results. This is judgement work, so a hosted model does it and I review the result.

→ sections added to paper.spans.json
STAGE 3

Write the dialogue

One hosted-model writer per part drafts the back-and-forth, working only from the paragraphs assigned to it. Each line records which paragraphs it drew on.

→ podcast/script.json
STAGE 4

Speak it

A C# service renders each line through the Windows speech engine, stitches the parts together, and writes a timestamp for every line back into the script.

→ part_01..06.wav

Here is what stage 1 actually produces. The <!-- p:N --> markers are HTML comments, so any Markdown reader ignores them and the working copy stays readable, but they are trivial to find with a regular expression.

Four papers have been through it

One paper has been all the way through. The other three stop after stage 1 because I have not sat down and run stage 2 on them. No queue, no blocker, just undone.

An aside, since people ask: the two roles rotate on an axis picked per paper, rather than one voice always asking and the other always answering. Across the 156 lines, 50 of which contain a question mark, it came out 30 questions to 20. Small thing, and it only exists because the first version had the opposite hardcoded into a prompt template.

The engineering

I cannot proofread 2,663 paragraphs, so the machine has to

This is the part that took the real work, and the reason is the same reason the project exists. Every stage above degrades its input in ways nobody catches by eye, and the person least able to catch them by eye is me.

So each stage writes a checksum alongside its output — a fingerprint that changes completely if any byte changes — and the paragraph index stamps the exact version of the text it describes. A stale index cannot quietly point at the wrong words. That makes the citations under each spoken line above mean something: they are checkable, so I checked them.

Re-running stage 1 over all four papers, twice each, reproduced every pinned checksum byte for byte.

What this result cannot tell you

It shows stage 1 is deterministic on this machine and that today's code still lands on checksums pinned weeks ago. It does not show stability across library versions, because the library version never changed between the pin and the check. A dependency bump is the case this test was built to catch and the case it has never seen.

It also says nothing about whether the extracted text is correct. Reproducing the same wrong answer twice is still reproducible, and the next section measures how often that happens.

Where it is weak

Roughly a fifth of the extracted paragraphs are damaged

Stage 1 reproduces perfectly and is not very good. Three recurring failure shapes, turned into three detectors and run across the whole corpus so the rate is a number rather than an impression.

Read the 22.9% carefully

That is the share of paragraphs with a detectable defect, not the share of the paper that is unusable. Most of the 504 stubs are figure-axis debris a reader skips. The 35 mangled decimals are the dangerous ones: a number reading 67 _._ 8 can be silently misread as 678 by anything that strips markup, and then a synthetic voice says it out loud with total confidence.

My detectors are three regular expressions written after seeing three failure shapes. They cannot find a fourth, and I have no estimate of how much they miss. The true rate is at least 22.9%.

And this table was wrong when I first published it

The first version of this page said 593 defects, 22.3%. Two readers noticed the per-paper columns did not sum to the totals and assumed deduplication of paragraphs hit by more than one detector. The deduplication was real and broken: my script collapsed duplicates by Python object identity over the paragraph text, and Python interns short strings, so every paragraph consisting of just '1' shared one identity and the group counted once. Real overlap is 6 paragraphs, not 22.

A page about checks that quietly lie, carrying a wrong number from a silent bug in its own measurement script. Left here rather than quietly fixed.

One more number the citations give up for free: the 156 spoken lines draw on 71 of the paper's 292 paragraphs, or 24%. Thirty-six minutes of audio covers roughly a quarter of the source. Whether that is compression or omission is not something the citations can answer, and I have not checked.

A bug worth the detour

The crackle that took a spectrum analyser to name

Stage 4 shipped audio with a fault I could hear and not describe: rapid small popping, "not quite fast enough to be static." Vague symptoms are where instrumentation pays for itself, because guessing has nowhere to start.

The Windows voices synthesise natively at 16,000 samples per second. A signal sampled that fast cannot carry anything above 8,000 Hz — that ceiling is called the Nyquist limit, and it is arithmetic, not a limitation of the equipment. So any energy an upsampled file shows above 8 kHz was invented by the conversion. Falsifiable, so I ran it: identical text, identical voice, four output settings.

A and C are byte-identical, which settles that the unspecified default was 22,050 Hz all along. Condition D exists because a reviewer pointed out that byte-identity does not prove a converter ran — the voice might simply be wideband. It is not. At 44,100 Hz, where a genuinely wideband voice would put real speech energy, there is nothing but junk 50 dB down. Every episode ever rendered had been pushed through a resampler for no reason. The fix was one argument, naming the rate the voice already uses. Files came out 27.4% smaller and lost nothing.

Below 8 kHz the two track within about 2 dB on average, with a few bins diverging up to 6 dB — these are two separate synthesis passes, not one resampled copy of the other, so some jitter is expected. Past 8 kHz the fixed render's data simply ends while the default keeps going at roughly −39 to −66 dB. That tail rides on sibilants, which is why it was audible on s sounds specifically.

Three different decibel numbers appear on this page. They are not the same measurement.

−36.5 dB is one sentence rendered today, voiced frames only. −39 to −66 dB is the per-bin range on the chart. Same phenomenon, two framings, and neither is comparable to the third one in the next paragraph.

The fix shipped with a source comment claiming the artifact sat "~120 dB over an ideal resample." I could not reproduce that. Measuring twelve legacy episode files whole, silence included, puts the artifact at −43.9 dB against an ideal-resample floor of −77.5 dB — an excess of 34 dB, not 120. But that floor is limited by leakage in my own estimator, so 34 dB is a lower bound, not a competing number. I cannot adjudicate it, and the 120 dB figure is sitting in a source comment where the next reader will believe it.

And I never verified the audible half. I measured a spectrum, not a listening test. The two clips above are the closest this page gets, and your ears are doing work mine has not.

A check that lied

Every line boundary is 2.8× longer than configured

Stage 4 writes a timestamp for every spoken line, which is what would let a reader UI highlight the paragraph being discussed. Verifying those timestamps is where I nearly fooled myself twice.

First attempt: compare each part's stated duration against the duration in the audio file's own header. Six parts, thirty-six minutes, difference 0.0 ms every time. A clean sweep, and almost meaningless — the renderer computes the stated total by summing the byte lengths of the files it wrote, and the finished file is a concatenation of those same files. Both sides divide the same byte count by the same byte rate. It proves concatenation dropped no frames. It cannot tell you whether a timestamp lands where the words are.

So I asked the audio instead: detect real silence in the waveform, and check whether it sits where the timestamps predict. Result, 150 of 150 boundaries within ±80 ms. Which is where I stopped — until four readers independently pointed out that a check never seen to fail is indistinguishable from a check that cannot fail. So I corrupted its input on purpose.

The rise from 40% at 700 ms back to 55% at 2,000 ms is not noise. A 700 ms shift lands the probe reliably inside the next line's speech, which is why it scores below chance; larger shifts decorrelate from line structure and drift back up to the 54.2% chance level. By 2,000 ms the check carries no signal at all.

The check cannot see half a second of drift. Every timestamp could be wrong by 500 ms and it would still report a perfect score, because the silence it looks for turned out to be 1,390 ms wide, so an ±80 ms probe stays inside it for any shift up to about 695 ms — half the gap.

It is not worthless. Against 20 draws of uniformly random positions the pass rate falls to 54.2% (sd 4.9), so the check does separate real timing from noise. But that 54.2% needs explaining, because a reader can and did do the arithmetic and get a contradiction: 150 gaps of 1,390 ms is only 9.5% of the runtime, so how does a random probe pass half the time? Because the boundaries are not the only silence. 28.3% of the episode is silent once sentence and clause pauses inside lines are counted. Predicting the null from that figure alone gives 53.8%, against 54.2% measured. Two independent derivations, and neither is in the original write-up, which is why the objection was fair.

Two proposed fixes, one of which does not work

A reader suggested the blind spot closes for the price of one constant: the real timestamps pass at ±10 ms too, so tighten the tolerance. Half right.

Tightening does sharpen the check a lot past 700 ms, from 40% down to 5%. It does nothing at all to the 500 ms blind spot, and the reason is geometric rather than fixable: the silence is 1,390 ms wide, so a probe displaced by less than half that is still inside the same silence no matter how narrow the probe is. The constant is worth changing and it does not close the hole.

The second suggestion was better and produced the sharpest result here. Shuffle the real timestamps among the boundaries, keeping the values and destroying only which boundary each belongs to. If the check is really validating correspondence it should collapse. It scores 100%, standard deviation zero, across 20 shuffles — and it must, because the check tests one instant in isolation and never consults which boundary it came from. Permuting a set the test reads as a set cannot change the answer.

So the proposed control is itself tautological

Which is the same defect as the 0.0 ms duration check this whole section exists to replace, arrived at one level up, by a reader who was right about the underlying property. The check is blind to boundary identity. It confirms that silence exists at 150 named instants, not that those are the right 150 instants in the right order. Detecting that needs a different instrument, not a different threshold, and I have not built one.

And that 1,390 ms is the actual finding, because the configuration asks for 500. The speech engine pads each per-line file with its own silence, and the renderer inserts its pause between two already-padded files.

Six percent of the episode is dead air nobody chose, and every conversational turn drags by nearly a second. You can hear it in the clip at the top. The knob works fine; turning it to zero would still leave a 900 ms gap, which is not what anyone reading the config would expect.

Not fixed, and here is what fixing it costs

The repair is to trim each per-line file to its voiced extent before stitching, which means the renderer takes on silence detection and a threshold that can be wrong. Get it wrong aggressively and you clip the start of words — a worse failure than slow pacing. That needs the listening test this project has never had, which is why it is still sitting here.

Unfinished

What is still missing

Three papers are ingested and have not been through stage 2. The reader interface that would use those per-line timestamps — highlighting the paragraph as the voices discuss it — does not exist yet; today the audio plays in a migration-era page kept alive for the purpose. And the pause fix above is known, specified, and unshipped.

There is also a seam that quietly stopped being true. The C# service tells a chat client how many paragraphs each paper has. It reports null, because that function is a deliberate placeholder written when stage 1 did not yet produce the data:

Stage 1 does produce it now, so the premise expired months ago and the interface has been under-reporting ever since. Refusing to fabricate was the right call and I would write it again: a null meaning "not implemented" is recoverable, a plausible wrong number is not. But a comment describing a temporary state has no way to notice when that state ends. Nothing failed. It just quietly stopped being true.

The gap that would have caught this, and everything else here

There is no test suite in this repository. Not a thin one, not a slow one. Every check on this page is a script written the day the page was written, which is why they found things and also why they found them months late. One assertion that the service reports as many sections as the index contains would have failed the day stage 1 shipped.

That is the honest summary: good at diagnosing its own failures after the fact, with nothing standing between it and the next one. These checks belong in continuous integration, and until they are there I have demonstrated archaeology, not prevention.

Provenance

Every figure here was measured on 9 September 2026 by re-running this repository: eight PDF extractions, five controlled speech renders (four of which are in the table above; the fifth, at 8,000 Hz, added nothing), a negative-control sweep over 150 line boundaries at four tolerances, 40 randomised nulls of two kinds, and spectral analysis over 73 rendered audio files and 2,663 anchored paragraphs on disk. Where a number disagrees with what the repository's own history claims, the disagreement is stated rather than resolved.

This page was revised after five readers reviewed it in isolation. Their corrections are visible above: the negative control exists because four of them asked for it, condition D because one proposed it, and the defect count is 609 rather than 593 because two checked whether a table added up.
